sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Tēzcatlīpōca** (*tezcatlipoca*) — The Smoking Mirror — belongs to the Nahuatl tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Night, Sorcery, Fate". The name means "Smoking mirror"[^1].

Tēzcatlīpōca is the Aztec night given will: the god of the obsidian mirror in which all things are seen, patron of rulers and sorcerers, tempter and destroyer of his own brother Quetzalcōātl. He is not evil — he is the shadow the world requires, and the Aztecs honoured him with their most terrible beauty: the year-long god made flesh.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Tēzcatlīpōca** and serves its temple at [tēzcatlīpōca.com](https://xn--tzcatlpca-bhb3yro.com). The restoration preserves a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — the macrons on ē, ī, and ō marking the long vowels — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *tezcatlipoca* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Tēzcatlīpōca** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "Smoking mirror"[^1].

The ASCII form *tezcatlipoca* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Tēzcatlīpōca** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — the macrons on ē, ī, and ō marking the long vowels — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **t** → **T** — Same
- **e** → **ē** — Macron: long /eː/
- **z** → **z** — Same
- **c** → **c** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same
- **i** → **ī** — Macron: long /iː/
- **p** → **p** — Same
- **o** → **ō** — Macron: long /oː/
- **c** → **c** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The project holds the domain **tēzcatlīpōca.com** (xn--tzcatlpca-bhb3yro.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/teːs.kat.liː.ˈpoː.ka/** — Classical Nahuatl.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: tehs-kaht-lee-POH-kah, long ō on the stressed penult.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Nahuatl** — Tēzcatlīpōca
- **His title** — Titlacahuan
- **Owned form** — Tēzcatlīpōca

Tēzcatlīpōca is Nahuatl for "Smoking Mirror": tēzcatl (mirror) + īpōca (smoking). The ē of tēzcatl, the ī of īpōca, and the final ō are all long — the macrons the restoration preserves — and the name belongs to the god of night, sorcery, rulership, and strife, whose obsidian mirror shows men themselves.

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual nahuatl names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Tēzcatlīpōca** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

In Aztec writing the name is a rebus: the smoking mirror itself — the obsidian disc with its scroll of smoke — worn at his temple or replacing his torn-off foot. The codices draw the name rather than spell it: the smoking mirror is both his glyph and his body.

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Tēzcatlīpōca is the Aztec night given will: the god of the obsidian mirror in which all things are seen, patron of rulers and sorcerers, tempter and destroyer of his own brother Quetzalcōātl. He is not evil — he is the shadow the world requires, and the Aztecs honoured him with their most terrible beauty: the year-long god made flesh.[^1]

### The Mirror

Obsidian polished to black glass: it shows the future, the hidden, and the viewer's true face.

### The Missing Foot

Torn off by the earth-monster Cipactli in the creation — the mirror smokes where the foot was.

### The First Sun

He was the sun of the first age — the jaguar sun — devoured with his world when it ended.

### The Ixiptla

At Toxcatl, a flawless youth lived as the god for a year — then climbed the temple steps to die as him.

sources.citation: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, General History of the Things of New Spain, 1577.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Tēzcatlīpōca concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The smoking mirror** — Knowledge of the hidden; the self seen without mercy
- **The jaguar** — His nahual — the night's power and the first sun's ferocity
- **The turkey** — His mocking disguise — the god who tests kings as a beggar
- **The black stripe** — The paint across his face — the night sky worn as war-color

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Tēzcatlīpōca's myths are all contest: with the earth-monster, with Quetzalcōātl, with the proud — he is the force that measures the strong by breaking them.[^1]

### The Foot in the Jaws (The Creation)

To make the world, Tēzcatlīpōca and Quetzalcōātl descended to the primordial waters where the caiman-monster Cipactli floated, all mouths. He offered his own foot as bait; the monster bit it off, and the two gods tore Cipactli apart — her body becoming the earth, her eyes the springs, her mouth the cave of creation. Every Aztec king thereafter ruled over ground purchased with the god's flesh.[^2]

### The Jaguar Sun (The Ages)

Tēzcatlīpōca was the first sun, Nahui Ocēlōtl, "Four Jaguar": his world of giants ended when Quetzalcōātl struck him from the sky, and jaguars devoured the people. Through the succession of suns the two brothers keep unmaking each other's worlds — the Aztec cosmos is their long quarrel, and the present fifth sun is only the latest armistice, held together by sacrifice.

### The Mirror Trick (The Fall of Tula)

Against Quetzalcōātl of Tōllān he came as a sorcerer: he showed the plumed god his true aged face in a mirror ("look at your flesh, lord"), tricked him into drunkenness and incest with his own sister, until the shamed god-king burned his palace and departed eastward on a raft of serpents. The Aztecs read the myth as history's engine: Tēzcatlīpōca destroys every golden age, and awaits it at the next shore.

### Toxcatl (The Festival)

Each year the Aztecs chose a flawless captive youth to be the ixiptla — the god's living image. For a year he walked as Tēzcatlīpōca: taught, adorned, honoured with four goddesses as wives. At the feast of Toxcatl he climbed the temple steps breaking his flutes one by one, and was offered at the summit — the most beautiful death in the Aztec year, and the empire's meditation on how divinity wears, and discards, the flesh.

sources.citation: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, General History of the Things of New Spain, 1577.
Frances Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl, University of Texas Press, 1983.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The friars made him the devil — Sahagún's own informants struggle with the comparison — but the colonial fusion was subtler: he survived in Nahua sorcery as lord of the crossroads and the dark arts, and in the Day of the Dead's night-side. Scholars compare him with the Maya Itzamna's shadow aspects and with every trickster-sovereign from Loki to Eshu: the god who governs by disrupting. Modern Mexican art and literature reclaimed him as the national shadow — Paz's "other Mexico."[^1]

Within the Nahuatl tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[cihuacoatl|Cihuacōātl]], [[coatlicue|Cōātlīcue]], [[huitzilopochtli|Huitzilopōchtli]], [[itzpapalotl|Itzpapālōtl]], [[mictlantecutli|Mictlāntēcutli]], and [[quetzalcoatl|Quetzalcōātl]].

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: "Smoking mirror" entered the world's vocabulary as the emblem of deceptive appearances. His obsidian mirror in the British Museum — Aztec-made, later owned by the Elizabethan magus John Dee as his scrying glass — is among the most storied objects on earth, linking Tenochtitlan to the court of Elizabeth I. Every account of Aztec civilization, from Prescott to the present, must reckon with his Toxcatl: the rite that made beauty, divinity, and death one ceremony.[^1]

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: His obsidian mirrors survive across collections — the British Museum's Dee mirror foremost — ground from the volcanic glass that Pachuca and Otumba supplied by the ton. The Florentine Codex's account of Toxcatl, illustrated by Nahua artists under Sahagún, is the fullest ritual description from the pre-Columbian world. Templo Mayor excavations found his cult's material traces among the offerings, and the Tizoc Stone and Calendar Stone's jaguar-sun glyph keeps his first age on the empire's central monuments.[^1]

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Florentine Codex
sections.body:
No Mesoamerican god collected more names — the Florentine Codex lists them like charges.

- **Titlacahuan** — 'He Whose Slaves We Are'; the sovereign title, said with bowed head.
- **Yoalli Ehécatl** — 'Night Wind'; the title under which he walks the crossroads.
- **Moyocoyatzin** — 'the Capricious One'; the creator who does as he pleases.
- **Necoc Yaotl** — 'Enemy of Both Sides'; the warrior's title, patron of strife itself.
- **Telpochtli** — 'the Young Man'; the title of his Toxcatl impersonator.
- **Yaotzin** — 'the Revered Enemy'; enmity itself, honoured.

sources.citation: Florentine Codex, Book 1 (Tezcatlipoca chapter).

sections.label: Aztec Sources
sections.body: His great seat was **Tenochtitlan**: south of the Templo Mayor stood his temple, where the Toxcatl ixiptla climbed to die, and the excavated offerings of the **Templo Mayor** — obsidian, jaguar bone, the sacrificial knives of his nights — keep his cult in the archaeology of the sacred precinct. At **Teotihuacan**, the Avenue of the Dead runs through the city his myth makes the site of the sun's creation; at **Tula**, the Toltec capital his legend overthrew, the warrior-columns of the morning-star temple mark Quetzalcōātl's defeat. His mirrors — the British Museum's John Dee mirror foremost — are his portable shrines, obsidian ground to show the hidden.

sources.citation: Templo Mayor excavation reports; Florentine Codex, Book 2 (Toxcatl).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Colonial-Era Sources
sections.body: The colonial file on him is the thickest of any god: **Sahagún's** twelve books return to him constantly (Book 1's chapter, Book 2's Toxcatl, Book 6's prayers); **Durán** gives the fullest calendar account of the ixiptla's year and death; **Motolinia**, **Torquemada**, and the **Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas** record the five-suns theology and the Tula legend. The friars made him the devil and preserved him in the act: the most demonized god of the conquest is, thanks to their diligence, the best documented.

sources.citation: Durán, Book of the Gods and Rites (Toxcatl); Sahagún, Florentine Codex.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Tēzcatlīpōca is the god of the honest mirror. He flatters no one: he shows the king his age, the golden age its end, the world its price. Every tradition needs a power that tests rather than comforts; the Aztecs gave him their most beautiful ceremonies, understanding that what breaks you falsely was never yours — and what survives the mirror is.[^1]

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.
